## Learning Objectives

:::{style="font-size: .8em"}
- Geometric interpretation of a basis
- Coordinates and coordinate vectors
- Uniqueness of coordinates
- Orthogonal sets and orthogonal bases
- Finding coordinates efficiently with an orthogonal basis
:::

## Coordinates Give Points Unique Names{.really-smaller-title}

:::{style="font-size: 1.em"}
:::{.center-text}
```{python}
import laUtilities as ut
import demoUtilities as dm
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import scipy as sp

ax = dm.plotSetup(-3,3,-3,3,size=(5,5))
ax.plot([0],[1],'ro',markersize=8)
ax.arrow(0, 0, 1, 0, head_width=0.2, head_length=0.2, length_includes_head = True)
ax.arrow(0, 0, 0, 1, head_width=0.2, head_length=0.2, length_includes_head = True)
ax.text(0.25,1,'(0,1)',size=20)
ax.plot([1],[0],'ro',markersize=8)
ax.text(1.25,0.25,'(1,0)',size=20)
ax.plot([-1],[2],'ro',markersize=8)
ax.text(-1.5,2.25,'(-1,2)',size=20);
```
:::
A coordinate system gives a _**unique name**_ to each point in a vector space. Traditionally, we label points using the standard basis. 
:::

## Coordinates as Movements Along Basis Vectors{.really-smaller-title}

:::{style="font-size: .8em"}
<!-- We write any point in space using coordinates, like $(-1, 2)$, but what do these coordinates represent?  -->

In our standard basis, the point $(-1, 2)$ means 

1. walk $-1$ in the direction of ${\bf e_1}$ and then 
2. walk $2$ in the direction of ${\bf e_2}$. 

In other words,

$$
(-1, 2) = -1 {\bf e_1} + 2 {\bf e_2}.
$$

In fact, _**any**_ $n$ linearly independent vectors in $\mathbb{R}^n$ can serve as a basis — giving a different coordinate system for the same space.
:::

## Unique Representation Theorem{.smaller-title}

:::{style="font-size: .8em"}

```{python}
from IPython.core.display import HTML

def generate_html():
    return r"""
    <div class="purple-box">
        <p><span class="label">Theorem</span>
         If we are given a basis for vector space \(H\), then each vector in \(H\) can be written in <em>only one way</em> as a linear combination of the basis vectors.
         </p>
    </div>
    """

html_content = generate_html()
display(HTML(html_content))
```

:::{.fragment}
__Proof.__ Suppose $\mathcal{B}\ = \{\mathbf{b}_1,\dots,\mathbf{b}_p\}$ is a basis for $H.$ In addition, suppose a vector $\mathbf{x}$ in $H$ can be generated in two ways:

$$
\mathbf{x} = c_1\mathbf{b}_1+\cdots+c_p\mathbf{b}_p \quad \text{and}
\quad
\mathbf{x} = d_1\mathbf{b}_1+\cdots+d_p\mathbf{b}_p.
$$
:::


:::{.fragment}
Subtracting gives ${\bf 0} = \mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x} = (c_1-d_1)\mathbf{b}_1+\cdots+(c_p-d_p)\mathbf{b}_p.$

Since $\mathcal{B}$ is a basis, the vectors $\mathbf{b}_1\dots\mathbf{b}_p$ are linearly independent. Hence, the weights in the above expression must all be zero. That is, $c_j = d_j$ for all $j$. As a result, the two representations must be the same.
:::
:::

```{python}
from IPython.core.display import HTML

def generate_html():
    return r"""
    <div class="blue-box">
        <p>Can a vector in \(V\) have two different \(\mathcal{B}\)-coordinate vectors for the same basis \(\mathcal{B}\)? Why or why not?</p>
    </div>
    """
display(HTML(generate_html()))
```

## Definition: B-Coordinates{.smaller-title}

:::{style="font-size: .75em"}

```{python}
from IPython.core.display import HTML

def generate_html():
    return r"""
    <div class="purple-box">
        <p>
         <span class="label">Coordinates and coordinate vectors</span>
         Suppose \(\mathcal{B}\ = \{\mathbf{b}_1,\dots,\mathbf{b}_p\}\) is a basis for vector space \(H\). For each \(\mathbf{x}\) in \(H\), the <b>coordinates</b> of \(\mathbf{x}\) relative to the basis \(\mathcal{B}\) are the weights \(c_1,\dots,c_p\) such that \(\mathbf{x} = c_1\mathbf{b}_1+\cdots+c_p\mathbf{b}_p\). <br><br> \([\mathbf{x}]_\mathcal{B} = \begin{bmatrix}c_1\\\vdots\\c_p\end{bmatrix} \) is called the <b>coordinate vector</b> of \(\mathbf{x}\) (relative to \(\mathcal{B}\)) or the <b>\(\mathcal{B}\)-coordinate vector</b> of \(\mathbf{x}\).
         </p>
    </div>
    """

html_content = generate_html()
display(HTML(html_content))
```

In $\mathbb{R}^2$, let's look at the point ${\bf x} = \begin{bmatrix}1\\6\end{bmatrix}$ in the standard basis and relative to a new basis $\mathcal{B} = \left\{\begin{bmatrix}1\\0\end{bmatrix}, \begin{bmatrix}1\\2\end{bmatrix}\right\}.$
:::


```{python}
# B-basis
fig = ut.two_d_figure('Dummylabel', xmin = xmin, xmax = xmax, ymin = ymin, ymax = ymax, size=(4.5,3.5))
m = b1[1]/b1[0]
upper_intercept = ymax - m * xmin
upper_intercept = b1[1] * np.ceil(upper_intercept / b1[1])
lower_intercept = ymin - m * xmax
lower_intercept = b1[1] * np.floor(lower_intercept / b1[1])
for yint in np.linspace(lower_intercept, upper_intercept, int((upper_intercept-lower_intercept)/b1[1])+1):
    fig.plotLinEqn(-b1[1], b1[0], yint, color = 'g', alpha=0.3)
for y in np.linspace(ymin, ymax, int(((ymax-ymin)/b1[1])+1)):
    fig.plotLinEqn(0., 1., y, color = 'g', alpha=0.3)
fig.plotLinEqn(b1[1], -b1[0], 0, color = 'k')
fig.plotLinEqn(b0[1], -b0[0], 0, color = 'k')
fig.plotPoint(0, 0, 'k')
fig.ax.text(0+.1, 0-.1, r'$\bf 0$', size = 12, horizontalalignment='left', verticalalignment='top')
fig.plotPoint(1, 0, 'g')
fig.ax.text(1+.1, 0-.1, r'${\bf b}_1$', size = 12, horizontalalignment='left', verticalalignment='top')
fig.plotPoint(b1[0], b1[1], 'g')
fig.ax.text(b1[0]+.1, b1[1]-.1, r'${\bf b}_2$', size = 12, horizontalalignment='left', verticalalignment='top')
fig.plotPoint(1, 6, 'b')
fig.ax.text(1+.1, 6-.1, r'${\bf x}$', size = 12, horizontalalignment='left', verticalalignment='top')
fig.ax.axis('off')
fig.ax.set_title('B-Basis. $[\mathbf{x}]_\mathcal{B}$ = (-2, 3)', size = 16);
```
:::

:::

:::
Notice that the _location_ of $\mathbf{x}$ relative to the origin does not change.  

Using the $\mathcal{B}$-basis, we get _different coordinates_. These are $[\mathbf{x}]_\mathcal{B} = \begin{bmatrix}-2\\3\end{bmatrix}$.
:::

## Finding B-Coordinates: Setup{.smaller-title}

:::{style="font-size: 1.em"}
__Example.__ Let $\mathbf{v}_1 = \begin{bmatrix}3\\6\\2\end{bmatrix}, \mathbf{v}_2 = \begin{bmatrix}-1\\0\\1\end{bmatrix}, \mathbf{x} = \begin{bmatrix}3\\12\\7\end{bmatrix},$ and $\mathcal{B} = \{\mathbf{v}_1,\mathbf{v}_2\}.$

<br>

Then $\mathcal{B}$ is a basis for $H$ = Span$\{\mathbf{v}_1,\mathbf{v}_2\}$ because $\mathbf{v}_1$ and $\mathbf{v}_2$ are linearly independent.

<br>

We want to determine if $\mathbf{x}$ is in $H$, and if it is, find the coordinate vector of $\mathbf{x}$ relative to $\mathcal{B}.$
:::

## Finding B-Coordinates: Row Reduction{.really-smaller-title}

:::{style="font-size: 1.em"}
If $\mathbf{x}$ is in $H,$ then the following vector equation is consistent:

$$
c_1\begin{bmatrix}3\\6\\2\end{bmatrix} + c_2\begin{bmatrix}-1\\0\\1\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}3\\12\\7\end{bmatrix}.
$$

If they exist, the scalars $c_1$ and $c_2,$ are the $\mathcal{B}$-coordinates of $\mathbf{x}.$

Row operations show that

$$
\left[ \begin{array}{cc|c}3&-1&3\\6&0&12\\2&1&7\end{array} \right] \sim \left[ \begin{array}{cc|c}1&0&2\\0&1&3\\0&0&0\end{array}\right].
$$

:::

## Visualizing B-Coordinates on a Subspace{.really-smaller-title}

:::{style="font-size: 1.em"}

The reduced row echelon form shows that the system is consistent, so $\mathbf{x}$ is in $H$ and $c_1 = 2$ and $c_2 = 3,$ so $[\mathbf{x}]_\mathcal{B} = \begin{bmatrix}2\\3\end{bmatrix}.$

:::{.center-text}
```{python}
#
qr_setting = None
fig = ut.three_d_figure((7, 7), fig_desc = 'Basis-B coordinate system on the subspace H', figsize = (6, 5),
                        xmin = -1, xmax = 10, ymin = -1, ymax = 10, zmin = -1, zmax = 14, qr = qr_setting)
v = [3.0, 6, 2]
u = [-1,  0, 1]
#
v = np.array([2, 0.5, 0.5])
u = np.array([1.,  2,   1])
fig.text(v[0], v[1]-0.75, v[2]-2, r'$\bf v_1$', 'v1', size=16)
fig.text(u[0]-0.5, u[1], u[2]+2, r'$\bf v_2$', 'v2', size=16)
fig.text(3*u[0]+2*v[0], 3*u[1]+2*v[1], 3*u[2]+2*v[2]+1, r'$\bf 2v_1+3v_2$', '2 v1 + 3 v2', size=16)
# plotting the span of v
fig.plotSpan(u, v, 'Green')
# blue grid lines
fig.plotPoint(0, 0, 0, 'y')
fig.plotPoint(u[0], u[1], u[2], 'b')
fig.plotPoint(2*u[0], 2*u[1], 2*u[2],'b')
fig.plotPoint(3*u[0], 3*u[1], 3*u[2], 'b')
fig.plotLine([[0, 0, 0], 4*u], color='b')
fig.plotLine([v, v+4*u], color='b')
fig.plotLine([2*v, 2*v+3*u], color='b')
fig.plotLine([3*v, 3*v+2.5*u], color='b')
# red grid lines
fig.plotPoint(v[0], v[1], v[2], 'r')
fig.plotPoint(2*v[0], 2*v[1], 2*v[2], 'r')
fig.plotPoint(3*v[0], 3*v[1], 3*v[2], 'r')
fig.plotLine([[0, 0, 0], 3.5*v], color='r')
fig.plotLine([u, u+3.5*v], color='r')
fig.plotLine([2*u, 2*u+3.5*v], color='r')
fig.plotLine([3*u, 3*u+2*v], color='r')
#
fig.plotPoint(3*u[0]+2*v[0], 3*u[1]+2*v[1], 3*u[2]+2*v[2], color='m')
# plotting the axes
fig.plotIntersection([0,0,1,0], [0,1,0,0], color='Black')
fig.plotIntersection([0,0,1,0], [1,0,0,0], color='Black')
fig.plotIntersection([0,1,0,0], [1,0,0,0], color='Black')
fig.set_title('Basis-B coordinate system on the subspace H', size=16)
```
:::

_Important:_ Don't be confused because the "coordinate axes" are not perpendicular. Really, _they don't need to be._

As long as the independent vectors span the space, there is only _one_ way to express any point in terms of them.

Thus, every point has a unique coordinate.
:::

## Practice: Finding B-Coordinates{.smaller-title}

```{python}
from IPython.core.display import HTML

def generate_html():
    return r"""
    <div class="blue-box">
        <p>Let \(\mathcal{B} = \{\mathbf{b}_1, \mathbf{b}_2\}\) with \(\mathbf{b}_1 = \begin{bmatrix}1\\1\end{bmatrix}\) and \(\mathbf{b}_2 = \begin{bmatrix}1\\-1\end{bmatrix},\) and let \(\mathbf{x} = \begin{bmatrix}4\\2\end{bmatrix}.\)
        <ol type="a">
            <li>Verify that \(\mathcal{B}\) is a basis for \(\mathbb{R}^2.\)</li>
            <li>Set up the linear system to find \([\mathbf{x}]_\mathcal{B}\) and solve it.</li>
            <li>Is \(\mathcal{B}\) an orthogonal basis? If so, use the efficient formula \(c_j = \frac{\mathbf{x}^\top \mathbf{b}_j}{\mathbf{b}_j^\top \mathbf{b}_j}\) to verify your answer.</li>
        </ol>
        </p>
    </div>
    """
display(HTML(generate_html()))
```

:::{.notes}
(a) b₁ and b₂ are not scalar multiples; det = −1−1 = −2 ≠ 0, so they form a basis.
(b) Solve c₁[1,1]ᵀ + c₂[1,−1]ᵀ = [4,2]ᵀ → c₁ = 3, c₂ = 1, so [x]_B = [3, 1]ᵀ.
(c) b₁·b₂ = 1(1)+1(−1) = 0, yes orthogonal. c₁ = (4+2)/2 = 3, c₂ = (4−2)/2 = 1. ✓
:::

## Definition: Orthogonal Sets{.smaller-title}

:::{style="font-size: .8em"}

```{python}
from IPython.core.display import HTML

def generate_html():
    return r"""
    <div class="purple-box">
        <p><span class="label">Orthogonal set</span>
        A set of vectors \(\small \{\mathbf{u}_1,\dots,\mathbf{u}_p\}\) in \(\mathbb{R}^n\) is said to be an <b>orthogonal set</b> if each pair of distinct vectors from the set is orthogonal, i.e., \(\small \mathbf{u}_i^\top \mathbf{u}_j = 0\;\;\mbox{if}\;i\neq j.\)
        </p>
    </div>
    """
html_content = generate_html()
display(HTML(html_content))
```

__Example.__  Consider

:::{style="font-size: .7em"}
$$
\mathbf{u}_1 = \begin{bmatrix}3\\1\\1\end{bmatrix},\;\;\mathbf{u}_2=\begin{bmatrix}-1\\2\\1\end{bmatrix},\;\;\mathbf{u}_3=\begin{bmatrix}-1/2\\-2\\7/2\end{bmatrix}.
$$
:::

:::

:::{style="font-size: .8em"}
We take the inner product of each pair of distinct vectors:
:::

:::{.fragment}
:::{style="font-size: .6em"}
$$\mathbf{u}_1^\top \mathbf{u}_2 = 3(-1) + 1(2) + 1(1) = 0. \checkmark$$
:::
:::

:::{.fragment}
:::{style="font-size: .6em"}
$$\mathbf{u}_1^\top \mathbf{u}_3 = 3(-1/2) + 1(-2) + 1(7/2) = 0. \checkmark$$
:::
:::

:::{.fragment}
:::{style="font-size: .6em"}
$$\mathbf{u}_2^\top \mathbf{u}_3 = -1(-1/2) + 2(-2) + 1(7/2) = 0. \checkmark$$
:::
:::

:::{.fragment}
:::{style="font-size: .8em"}
Hence, $\small \{\mathbf{u}_1,\mathbf{u}_2, \mathbf{u}_3\}$ is an orthogonal set.
:::
:::

## Definition: Orthogonal Basis{.smaller-title}

:::{style="font-size: .8em"}
```{python}
from IPython.core.display import HTML

def generate_html():
    return r"""
    <div class="purple-box">
        <p><span class="label">Orthogonal basis</span>
       An <b>orthogonal basis</b> for a subspace \(H\) of \(\mathbb{R}^n\) is a <em>basis</em> for \(H\) that is also an <em>orthogonal set</em>.
        </p>
    </div>
    """
html_content = generate_html()
display(HTML(html_content))
```

Consider,

$$
\mathbf{u}_1 = \begin{bmatrix} -1/2\\ 2\\ 1 \end{bmatrix},
\mathbf{u}_2 = \begin{bmatrix} 8/3\\ 1/3\\ 2/3 \end{bmatrix}.
$$

Since, $\mathbf{u}_1^\top \mathbf{u}_2 = 0,$ they form an orthogonal basis for subspace $\mbox{Span}\{\mathbf{u}_1,\mathbf{u}_2\}.$
:::

## Computing Coordinates: General Method{.really-smaller-title}

:::{style="font-size: .8em"}
To compute the coordinates of $\mathbf{y}$ in terms of basis $\mathcal{B} = \{\mathbf{u}_1,\mathbf{u}_2, \mathbf{u}_3\}$, $[\mathbf{y}]_\mathcal{B}$, we need to solve the linear system:

$$
c_1 \mathbf{u}_1 + c_2\mathbf{u}_2 + c_3\mathbf{u}_3 = \mathbf{y}
$$

or

$$
U\mathbf{c} = \mathbf{y}.
$$

In general, to solve the system we'd need to perform Gauss-Jordan Elimination that takes on the order of $n^3$ floating point operations.

<br>

However, in an orthogonal basis the coordinates of any point can be computed more efficiently.
:::

## Efficient Coordinates via Orthogonal Basis{.really-smaller-title}

:::{style="font-size: .8em"}
```{python}
from IPython.core.display import HTML

def generate_html():
    return r"""
    <div class="purple-box">
        <p><span class="label">Theorem</span>
        Let \(\{\mathbf{u}_1,\dots,\mathbf{u}_p\}\) be an orthogonal basis for a subspace \(H\) of \(\mathbb{R}^n\). For each \(\mathbf{y}\) in \(H\), the weights of the linear combination \(c_1\mathbf{u}_1 + \dots + c_p\mathbf{u}_p = \mathbf{y}\) are given by \(c_j = \frac{\mathbf{y}^\top \mathbf{u}_j}{\mathbf{u}_j^{\top} \mathbf{u}_j}\) with \(j = 1,\dots,p.\)
        </p>
    </div>
    """
html_content = generate_html()
display(HTML(html_content))
```

__Proof.__  Let's consider the inner product of $\mathbf{y}$ and one of the $\mathbf{u}$ vectors --- say, $\mathbf{u}_1$.

The orthogonality of $\{\mathbf{u}_1,\dots,\mathbf{u}_p\}$ means that

$$\small \begin{align*}
\mathbf{y}^\top \mathbf{u}_1 &= (c_1\mathbf{u}_1 + c_2\mathbf{u}_2 + \dots + c_p\mathbf{u}_p)^\top \mathbf{u}_1 \\
&= c_1(\mathbf{u}_1^\top \mathbf{u}_1).
\end{align*}
$$

Since $\mathbf{u}_1^\top \mathbf{u}_1$ is not zero, the equation above can be solved as $c_1 = \frac{\mathbf{y}^\top \mathbf{u}_1}{\mathbf{u}_1^\top \mathbf{u}_1}.$
To find any other $c_j,$ compute $\mathbf{y}^\top \mathbf{u}_j$ and solve for $c_j$.

:::

```{python}

    </div>
    """
display(HTML(generate_html()))
```

## Expressing a Vector in an Orthogonal Basis{.really-smaller-title}

:::{style="font-size: .8em"}
__Example__. The set $S$ that we saw earlier,

$$
\mathbf{u}_1 = \begin{bmatrix}3\\1\\1\end{bmatrix},\;\;\mathbf{u}_2=\begin{bmatrix}-1\\2\\1\end{bmatrix},\;\;\mathbf{u}_3=\begin{bmatrix}-1/2\\-2\\7/2\end{bmatrix},
$$

is an orthogonal basis for $\mathbb{R}^3.$

Let's express $\mathbf{y} = \begin{bmatrix}6\\1\\-8\end{bmatrix}$ as a linear combination of the vectors in $S.$

That is, find $\mathbf{y}$'s coordinates in the basis $S$ --- i.e., in the coordinate system $S$.
:::

## Computing Orthogonal Basis Coordinates: Example{.really-smaller-title}

:::{style="font-size: .8em"}
__Example__. Compute

$$
\mathbf{y}^\top \mathbf{u}_1 = 11,\;\;\;\mathbf{y}^\top \mathbf{u}_2 = -12,\;\;\;\mathbf{y}^\top \mathbf{u}_3 = -33,
$$

$$
\mathbf{u}_1^\top \mathbf{u}_1 = 11,\;\;\;\mathbf{u}_2^\top \mathbf{u}_2 = 6,\;\;\;\mathbf{u}_3^\top \mathbf{u}_3 = 33/2.
$$

$$
\begin{align*}
\Rightarrow \mathbf{y} &= \frac{\mathbf{y}^\top \mathbf{u}_1}{\mathbf{u}_1^\top \mathbf{u}_1}\mathbf{u}_1 + \frac{\mathbf{y}^\top \mathbf{u}_2}{\mathbf{u}_2^\top \mathbf{u}_2}\mathbf{u}_2 + \frac{\mathbf{y}^\top \mathbf{u}_3}{\mathbf{u}_3^\top \mathbf{u}_3}\mathbf{u}_3 \\
&= \left(\frac{11}{11}\right)\mathbf{u}_1 + \left(\frac{-12}{6}\right)\mathbf{u}_2 + \left(\frac{-33}{33/2}\right)\mathbf{u}_3 \\
&= \mathbf{u}_1 - 2\mathbf{u}_2 - 2 \mathbf{u}_3.
\end{align*}
$$

Hence, $[{\bf y}]_{\mathcal{B}} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -2 & -2 \end{bmatrix}^\top$.

:::

## Why Orthogonal Bases Are Computationally Efficient{.really-smaller-title}

:::{style="font-size:.8em"}

Finding the coordinates of $\mathbf{y}$ in the orthogonal basis is efficient because

- There are $2n$ inner products, each requiring $2n$ flops.
- Each coefficient $c_i$ can be calculated separately, allowing for parallel computation in linear time.

## Isomorphisms

:::{style="font-size: .8em"}
```{python}
from IPython.core.display import HTML

def generate_html():
    return r"""
    <div class="purple-box">
        <p>
         When we have a one-to-one correspondence between two subspaces that preserves linear combinations, we call such a correspondence an <b>isomorphism,</b> and we say that \(H\) is <b>isomorphic</b> to \(\mathbb{R}^2.\)
         </p>
    </div>
    """

html_content = generate_html()
display(HTML(html_content))
```

<br>

In general, if $\mathcal{B}\ = \{\mathbf{b}_1,\dots,\mathbf{b}_p\}$ is a basis for $H$, then the mapping $\mathbf{x} \mapsto [\mathbf{x}]_\mathcal{B}$ is a one-to-one correspondence that makes $H$ look and act the same as $\mathbb{R}^p.$   

<br>

This is _even through the vectors in $H$ themselves may have more than $p$ entries._
::: -->

## Looking Ahead: Projection{.smaller-title}

:::{style="font-size: 1em"}
We've seen two key benefits of orthogonal bases:

1. **Coordinates** are easy to compute: $c_j = \dfrac{\mathbf{y}^\top \mathbf{u}_j}{\mathbf{u}_j^\top \mathbf{u}_j}$ — no matrix inversion needed.

2. In the next lecture, we'll see that orthogonal bases also make **projection** easy — finding the closest point in a subspace to any vector.
:::
